title: Chapter 58 — Brit
paragraphs: Steering northeast from the Crozets, we fell in with vast meadows of brit, the minute, yellow substance upon which the Right Whale largely feeds. For league upon league it undulated around us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe, golden wheat.

On the second day, numbers of Right Whales were seen, who — safe from the attack of a Sperm Whaler like the Pequod — with open jaws sluggishly swam through the brit. It clung to the fringing fibers of that wondrous Venetian blind in their mouths, and was in this way separated from the water that escaped at the lip.

As morning mowers, who side by side slowly and steadily advance their scythes through the long wet grass of marshy meadows — even so these monsters swam, making a strange, grassy, cutting sound and leaving behind them endless swaths of blue upon the yellow sea.

That part of the sea known among whalemen as the "Brazil Banks" does not bear that name because of shallows and soundings there, as the Banks of Newfoundland do, but because of this remarkable meadow-like appearance, caused by the vast drifts of brit continually floating in those latitudes, where the Right Whale is often hunted.

But it was only the sound they made as they parted the brit that reminded one of mowers at all. Seen from the mastheads, especially when they paused and were still for a while, their vast black forms looked more like lifeless masses of rock than anything else. And as in the great hunting countries of India, the stranger at a distance will sometimes pass elephants lying on the plains without recognizing them, mistaking them for bare, blackened humps of earth — so, often, with whales.

Indeed, in other respects, you can hardly regard any creatures of the deep with the same feelings as those of the shore. For though some old naturalists have maintained that all creatures of the land have their counterparts in the sea — and though, taking a broad general view, this may be true — yet when it comes to specifics, where, for example, does the ocean offer any fish that in temperament matches the loyal kindness of the dog? The cursed shark alone can in any way be compared to him. But as for the gentle whale — what has he in common with anything ashore?

But though, to landsmen in general, the native inhabitants of the seas have always been regarded with feelings unspeakably hostile and repelling — though we know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so that Columbus sailed over numberless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one — though by vast odds the most terrible of all mortal disasters have from time immemorial fallen indiscriminately upon tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone upon the waters — though the sea has been the sworn enemy of man since man was man — yet man has always gone to sea and always will.

The first boat we read of floated on an ocean that with Portuguese vengeance had drowned a whole world without leaving so much as a widow. That same ocean rolls now. That same ocean destroyed the wrecked ships of last year. Yes, foolish mortals — Noah's flood has not yet subsided. Two thirds of the fair world it still covers.

How do the sea and the land differ, that a miracle upon one is not a miracle upon the other? Supernatural terrors seized the Hebrews when under the feet of Korah and his company the living ground opened and swallowed them up forever. Yet not a modern sun ever sets but in precisely the same manner the living sea swallows up ships and crews.

But not only is the sea such a foe to man, who is alien to it — it is also a fiend to its own offspring. Worse than the Persian host who murdered his own guests, it does not spare the creatures it has itself produced. Like a savage tigress that, tossing in the jungle, crushes her own cubs, so the sea dashes even the mightiest whales against the rocks, and leaves them there side by side with the split wrecks of ships. No mercy, no power but its own controls it. Panting and snorting like a mad battle horse that has lost its rider, the masterless ocean overruns the globe.

Consider the subtlety of the sea — how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, invisible for the most part, treacherously hidden beneath the loveliest shades of blue. Consider also the devilish brilliance and beauty of many of its most merciless species, like the elegantly shaped bodies of many kinds of sharks. Consider, once more, the universal cannibalism of the sea: all whose creatures prey upon each other, waging eternal war since the world began.

Consider all this, and then turn to this green, gentle, and most docile earth. Consider them both — the sea and the land — and do you not find a strange parallel to something in yourself? For as this appalling ocean surrounds the green land, so in the soul of man there lies one island Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but surrounded by all the horrors of the half-known life. God keep you! Push not off from that island — you can never return!
